chapter_theme: Power belongs to the ground it stands on. Through animals and vehicles, the chapter shows the strong undone off their own ground and the weak made strong on theirs, and it warns against attacking even people with nothing but their home.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: the place for besieging (491-494), the place for acting (495-497), and places not to approach and the cost of doing so (498-500).

491.reading: Begin no deed and scorn nothing until you have seen the ground for it in full.

positions.position: முற்றும் is a verb, to besiege: don't act against an enemy until you have ground for a siege.
positions.quote: பகைவரை முற்றுதற்கு ஆவதோர் இடம் பெற்றபின் அல்லது;

positions.position: முற்றும் is to complete: don't begin any deed until you see where it can be finished, and don't treat it as easy.
positions.quote: முடியுமிடங் கண்டாலல்லது, யாதொரு வினையுந் தொடங்கா தொழிக; எளிதென்றிகழாதொழிக,

positions.position: முற்றும் is 'fully': choose a completely right place.
positions.quote: முற்றிலும் சரியான இடத்தைத் தேர்ந்தெடுத்து அச்செயலில் இறங்க வேண்டும்.

492.reading: Even for those of contentious strength, the gain that comes by joining a fortress gives many benefits.
492.nuance: Even the strong: உம் concedes the objection. Manakkudavar takes the fort as one's own place, and Parimelazhagar, who thinks of a king on campaign, as a siege position. Either way, it is a protection for those who think they don't need it.

493.reading: Even those without strength become strong and win, if they know the place and act against foes while guarding themselves.
493.nuance: The ஆற்றி in ஆற்றாரும் ஆற்றி plays on the same root: place does not merely help the weak but turns them into the strong.

494.reading: Those who had planned will lose their plan, if those who approach know the place and hold to it.
494.nuance: The loss is of a thought: the enemy's victory has been defeated before fighting starts.

positions.position: துன்னியார் are the kings who have marched there and who stay close to their fort.
positions.quote: தாம் வினை செய்தற்கு ஏற்ற இடத்தினை அறிந்து சென்ற அரசர்;

positions.position: துன்னியார் are allies acting with one mind, so the verse is about concord among friends as well as place.
positions.quote: வினைசெய்யும் இடமறிந்து நட்டோரானவர் மனம் பொருந்திச் செய்வாராயின்.

495.reading: A crocodile wins in deep water; if it leaves the water, others kill it.
495.nuance: The very same animal, and the reversal is total: பிற, anything at all. Parimelazhagar's maxim is that everyone is strong on their own ground, and the practical point is to fight where the enemy can't stand.

496.reading: Long chariots with strong wheels don't run on the sea; ships that run on the sea don't run on land.
496.nuance: The verse states an obvious fact without comment, and the plainness is the point. Parimelazhagar notes the qualities listed, strong wheels and great size, as just those that don't transfer. He and Manakkudavar read it as being about fitting equipment to the terrain.

497.reading: No support is needed but fearlessness, if you think everything through and act by the place.
497.nuance: This verse suggests an answer to how 382's fearlessness can sit with 428's fear of what should be feared: fearlessness is what remains once the thinking is complete, எஞ்சாமை எண்ணி. Parimelazhagar glosses அஞ்சாமை as firmness.

498.reading: If one with a large army enters where one with a small army can move, his zeal is destroyed.
498.nuance: The large army's size becomes the problem. Parimelazhagar explains that it can't act together and has no practice on that ground. What is destroyed is ஊக்கம், the fighting spirit, not only the force.

499.reading: Even if they have no fortress or standing, it is hard to take on people on the land where they live.
499.nuance: Parimelazhagar sees the reason in psychology: attacked at home, such people won't resolve to flee; they will resolve to die, and even a large army breaks on that. The verse says மாந்தர், people, not soldiers.

500.reading: The jackal kills, in mud where feet sink, the unflinching elephant with a warrior's face.
500.nuance: The chapter closes with its most extreme reversal, the jackal over the elephant. கண் அஞ்சா also splits the commentators, between a beast unafraid at a glance and one that won't obey its handlers.

positions.position: The elephant is one that strikes down spearmen. He rejects the variant வேலாழ், because a wounded elephant makes the jackal's success unremarkable.
positions.quote: 'வேலாழ் முகத்த' என்று பாடம் ஓதுவாரும் உளர்; வேற்படை குளித்த முகத்தவாயின் அதுவும் நரி அடுதற்கு ஏதுவாய் முடிதலின், அது பாடம் அன்மை அறிக.

positions.position: The elephant's face has spears sunk in it: he follows the variant reading.

links.note: The crow beats the owl by day and the crocodile wins in water. Time and place are two axes of the same argument: strength isn't an attribute of a creature but of a creature in a circumstance.

In Parimelazhagar's reading, 471 says to act only if your side is stronger. 493 says the weak can win by choosing the ground. If so, the calculation of 471 must already have place in it, or 471's rule is too strict.

444 calls greater people as support the chief of all strengths; 497 says no support is needed but fearlessness, if the thinking and place are right. A chapter later, the book seems to take back its own superlative.

A great elephant is undone in both: by a tiger's spirit in 599 and by a jackal in the mud here. One verse credits the attacker's ஊக்கம் and the other only the ground, so size loses for two quite different reasons.
